scenes.intent: Set up the central problem: CTM is compact while super-resolution needs dense spatial output.
scenes.claim: Compact thought clashes with dense reconstruction.
scenes.narration: CTM carries its reasoning in a compact state, which is useful for control but thin for image restoration. Super-resolution asks for a value at every spatial location, so the model must preserve local detail while it reasons.

objects.text: Compact thought clashes with dense reconstruction.

scenes.intent: Show the two existing adaptations and why neither resolves the mismatch cleanly.
scenes.claim: Direct adaptations leave the mismatch exposed.
scenes.narration: A plain CTM keeps the thought compact, so the dense image field is not represented directly. A window-wise adaptation brings CTM into patches, but the dense carrier is still not persistent across the reconstruction.

objects.text: Direct adaptations leave the mismatch exposed.

scenes.intent: Introduce the persistent dense carrier as the core idea.
scenes.claim: ThinkSR keeps a dense carrier alive while it thinks.
scenes.narration: The method starts by encoding the low-resolution image into a feature field. That field is split into windows, giving compact thought a dense place to read from and write back to. The carrier persists through repeated ticks instead of being rebuilt from isolated window outputs.

objects.text: ThinkSR keeps a dense carrier alive while it thinks.

scenes.intent: Walk through the end-to-end architecture from encoder to decoder.
scenes.claim: The architecture routes dense features through shared ticks.
scenes.narration: ThinkSR encodes the low-resolution input before any compact reasoning happens. Windows then pass through shared DQ-CTM ticks, so repeated processing updates the same dense representation. A decoder finally turns the updated carrier into the super-resolved output.

objects.text: The architecture routes dense features through shared ticks.

scenes.intent: Explain repeated updates as the mechanism for improving a dense reconstruction.
scenes.claim: Repeated ticks refine the same reconstruction state.
scenes.narration: The reconstruction begins before the shared ticks have done their work. Each tick updates the same state, so improvement is expressed as accumulated changes rather than separate predictions. The sequence from T equals zero through T equals four shows the model moving toward the target reconstruction.

objects.text: Repeated ticks refine the same reconstruction state.

scenes.intent: Use the error-map figure to explain how the method is judged spatially.
scenes.claim: The method is judged by where reconstruction error remains.
scenes.narration: The paper compares reconstructions with absolute-error maps on the same image crops. A shared colour scale makes the remaining error directly comparable across methods. This matters because super-resolution quality is spatial, not just a single score.

objects.text: The method is judged by where reconstruction error remains.

scenes.intent: Summarize the benchmark table without inventing additional metrics.
scenes.claim: DQ-CTM-SR lands in the CNN-baseline range.
scenes.narration: Across the five-benchmark average, DQ-CTM-SR reports twenty eight point nine eight three with one point one two nine million parameters. CARN and IMDN are essentially the same average range, while RFDN is slightly higher. CATANet is the strongest listed method, with a higher average and fewer parameters than DQ-CTM-SR.

objects.text: DQ-CTM-SR lands in the CNN-baseline range.

scenes.intent: Explain the main cost: the dense carrier adds parameters and still trails newer transformer baselines.
scenes.claim: The dense carrier helps, but it is not the lightest winner.
scenes.narration: DQ-CTM-SR uses one point one two nine million parameters in the reported comparison. CATANet is listed with zero point five three five million parameters and the highest average in the table. The result is competitive with CNN baselines, but it remains behind recent lightweight transformers.

objects.text: The dense carrier helps, but it is not the lightest winner.

scenes.intent: Clarify why the idea works conceptually: compact reasoning acts through a dense memory rather than replacing it.
scenes.claim: The key move is separating memory from reasoning.
scenes.narration: The dense carrier stores spatial information, while compact thought performs the repeated reasoning step. This split lets CTM-style processing touch every window without collapsing the reconstruction into a single compact vector. The model therefore keeps the spatial field available until decoding.

objects.text: The key move is separating memory from reasoning.

scenes.intent: Position the contribution honestly between CNN baselines and lightweight transformers.
scenes.claim: ThinkSR is a bridge, not a final benchmark leader.
scenes.narration: The result supports the idea that compact thought can be adapted to super-resolution. Its average is competitive with established CNN baselines in the table. The same table and summary keep the limit clear: recent lightweight transformers still lead this comparison.

objects.text: ThinkSR is a bridge, not a final benchmark leader.

scenes.intent: Close with the ordered takeaway: problem, idea, evidence, cost.
scenes.claim: The contribution is a dense home for compact thought.
scenes.narration: The problem is that CTM reasoning is compact while super-resolution is dense. ThinkSR answers by keeping a persistent dense carrier that compact thought can update through windows and ticks. The evidence says this is competitive with CNN baselines, while stronger lightweight transformer results still define the upper benchmark.

objects.text: The contribution is a dense home for compact thought.
